utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Thayer, we're ready for you to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to you and Your Honours. Good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, good morning.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to stay on this day, the 25th of May, 1995, we spoke a little bit about yesterday. Following the NATO air strikes on VRS facilities, we spoke a little bit about the shelling that occurred of Sarajevo and the enclaves. I want to just read you a small passage from a lengthy Dutch investigation report, the NIAD report that everybody here is familiar with?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 3970. It's part 3, chapter 5, section 2. We don't need to put it up on e-court. I'll just read it. It's very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "Much of the Bosnian Serb revenge following the NATO bombing of Pale on 25 and 26 May concentrated on Sarajevo, but the eastern enclaves were not spared. This also had repercussions on the situation around Srebrenica. "On 25 May, as immediate retaliation, a number of shells landed close to a school in Srebrenica. There were one dead and three wounded. The VRS also opened fire on the southwestern part of the enclave." Now, General, we have the Bratunac Brigade daily combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could have P03359.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll let you take a look at that. General, this is an interim combat report from the 25th of May from Commander Blagojevic of the Bratunac Brigade. Paragraph 1, as you can see says: "In accordance with an oral order from Colonel Lazic, we fired two shells from two 105 millimetre Howitzers (a total of four shells) on the town of Srebrenica at 1907 hours. Artillery observers at Pribicevac reported that two shells fell near the Domavija feature. The other two shells were not observed, but they fell on Srebrenica." Now, I just want to put a couple of additional facts to you and then ask you a question. One of those shells, General, killed nine-year-old Jazna Gabelic who was in her home in Srebrenica when the shell struck it; and her sister, Alma, who was seriously wounded, has testified. And I would like to show you one more document and then put my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's 5D1161.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What we have here, General, is a report from the Main Staff, a daily report to the president, Dr. Karadzic, for the 25th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we go to page 3 of the B/C/S, and that's going to be page 4 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you look at paragraph 6, in particular 6(b), the situation in the corps, do you see that, General, that section?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It says: "Artillery fire was opened on the Srebrenica and Gorazde enclaves as well as the Tuzla airport." Now, General, again I put it to you that these different subordinate units, firing on Sarajevo, Srebrenica town, Gorazde, and Tuzla, didn't just coincidentally decide to shell all at the same time, but were ordered to do so by the Main Staff. As chief of artillery of the Main Staff, General, at the time, what is your response to that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen a single document which says that the Main Staff ordered fire to be open on the protected areas at the same time; i.e., I've not read in any document that the Main Staff ordered fire to be opened at the time at all. I explained to you yesterday that every unit has, under its immediate command, artillery units, and that every command is autonomous, and also that the commander of every unit has the right to decide when and how, with what weapons, to open fire. Only if there is a cease-fire, in that situation they will turn to the superior command to ask for their approval. I don't see anywhere here that the Main Staff ordered fire to be observed at the time in a synchronised manner targeting these particular facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, my question wasn't whether you saw it in any document or report. My question was: You were chief of artillery of the Main Staff at the time. Was this shelling on the 25th of May, which occurred after the NATO air strikes that day, ordered by the Main Staff? That's my question, whether you have any knowledge of that, whether it was ordered by the Main Staff; not whether you just saw it in some report or not.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not an order by the Main Staff issued at the time. Somebody may have ordered fire to be opened on certain targets; however, when it comes to these particular activities, this was not proceeded by an order from the Main Staff. In any case, the order - if there was one - did not come from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, if you could give me the reference of the testimony of Alma, whose nine-year-old brother was killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It was her nine-year-old sister, Mr. President, and that was admitted pursuant to 92 bis in this case by the Court's decision back in, I believe, September of 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, General, it's your testimony, then, before this Trial Chamber that all of this firing which occurred on the 25th of May occurred coincidentally on the part of individual decisions made by subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, the commanders did receive certain orders, I suppose from the commander of the Main Staff, as to what activities should be under taken. As for the order to open fire, that order did not come from the Main Staff and nobody in the Main Staff specified any targets or any particular times at which fire should be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me make sure I understand your testimony correctly, General. Are you telling the Trial Chamber that it is your understanding that the orders or the order to fire on the 25th of May came from General Mladic and not from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that General Mladic issued an order to that effect or not. I was not there to hear General Mladic issuing any order of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But, if I understand you correctly, General, the reason why you just told us that, and I'll quote you, "In any case, the commanders did receive certain orders, I suppose from the commanders of the Main Staff, as to which activities should be undertaken," is that surely you recognise that the possibility that all of this fire at the same time on the eastern enclaves could not have been coincidental. That is why you are trying to identify somebody who must have given the order to open that fire. Is that what you're telling the Trial Chamber, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not see well, and I did not notice that there was simultaneous fire opened on the enclaves. If there had been simultaneous fire, as you claim, and if there is a document or a report that the fire was opened simultaneously, then somebody had ordered for fire to be opened at that same time. If the fire was not synchronised and simultaneous, I am telling you again that it is within the exclusive purview of the commander to issue such an order within their normal competences to decide when to open fire and at what targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. But, General, we just saw the daily combat report from the Bratunac Brigade which specifically stated that they have received their orders to fire upon an oral order from Colonel Lazic, who was chief of operation of training at the Drina Corps. Now, he's not an artillery guy, so who's giving him the order? Who is in the position to give him the order to pass on to the Bratunac Brigade on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the chief or the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we are talking about coordinated fire, who is going to be giving the order to the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, General Masal. Ms. Fauveau Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could one specify about coordinated fire what unit one is talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think it's clear what we are talking about here, and I think the General understands what I've been talking about. We've been vague a conversation about this for the last 20 minutes, so if I may continue and just get an answer to my question, which was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand the question to be asking you whether it was a coordinated operation among the corps, because this refers to the Drina Corps only.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, and the thrust of my questioning, as we have fired, as we heard from the section from the NIAD report, that there was fire opened up on Sarajevo as well, which involves the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. So my question is, if we are talking about a coordinated response in response to the NATO air strikes, my question to the General is: Who is in the position to order these corps to open that fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Your explanation clarified your question. I think now the General is in the position to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want the true answer to your question as to whether the Main Staff coordinated the artillery fire on Sarajevo and Srebrenica as well as Gorazde and Tuzla, then we need to have the information that an order was issued at the same time to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the Drina Corps, and the East Bosnian Corps to open artillery fire on the aforementioned sectors. You have provided me with a document which speaks about the shelling of Srebrenica which is within the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade which is on the strength of the Drina Corps. There is no need for the commander of the Main Staff, and that would be -- not be within the principle of command and control to issue order to the Bratunac Brigade to open fire, for example, at 1500 hours. In other words, I don't see any sort of the coordination in all of this. I am not excludeing the possibility that somebody may have ordered to the commander of the Drina Corps, Colonel Blagojevic, to open fire, or maybe the commander of the Sarajevo Corps -- Sarajevo Drina Corps opened his subordinate to open fire. But I don't see that General Mladic or his deputy in the Main Staff saw it fit to assume such a role in -- in this situation. I don't see it anywhere in any of your documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, my question to you was quite simple, and nobody is suggesting that General Mladic picked up the phone and called the Bratunac Brigade artillery chief. To the contrary, as we have been talking about, the order, as we could see from that combat report, to fire came from an oral order from Colonel Lazic out of the ops and training administration of the Drina Corps. So my question to you is simple: When we are talking about fire being opened up by multiple corps, who is going to be giving that order if multiple corps are meant to be engaged at or about the same time? That's simple question to you. Is it you? Is it someone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was opening at the same time, the exclusive right to issue order is to the -- lies with the corps commander or his deputy. I did not have the right to issue orders for corps activities if those activities were coordinated. If it was done over a period of time, then this could have been a coincidence rather than a coordinated activity. If this had been coordinated, then it would be to the minute if not to the second when fire was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll try one more time, General. If it had been coordinated, who would have given the order to the corps? Where would that order come from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness answered this question, page 8, lines 11, 12, and 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Mr. President, he has not answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think he has answered the question, but albeit speculative. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If somebody had ordered this, then it would be the commander of the Main Staff or his deputy who would have the exclusive right to order such a thing to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, last Friday you testified, and let me just quote you directly from the transcript, and this is at 29028. You said: "What I am aware of, and I do know this, is that in all orders, and especially in preparing combat activities, emphasis was always laid on taking into account possible casualties among the civilian population and reduce such casualties to a minimum especially in built up areas, or to avoid them if at all possible." Do you recall that testimony, General? I just want to refresh your recollection about it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that your basic task was to see that the artillery units were properly used in the units lower down; and to take care and keep records of their technical equipment, the artillery, ammunition; and to be in control of the artillery cadres, that is, the men; and to make proposals for promotions, training, and moving people around.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, finally, just one last thing. You also testified that you toured the corps and, and I quote: "And I make proposals to the corps commanders instructing them how they should deal with the situation and also to report back to General Milovanovic about the situation." Do you remember testifying to that effect yesterday at 29100 of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it was a general statement. I think it had to do with the Operation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you refer to Spreca?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think that's the case at all. If you look at the answer that General Masal gave, it was in response to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You could give a more detailed reference to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: A very general --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- so that he could taken question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I asked you yesterday, at page 29.100, "Can you give us an he idea, and let's start from the bottom up, when authorisation was required or not for artillery assets to be employed ..." -- let me withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: One second. Wrong question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me read the correct question that I asked you. I asked you: "Presumably on your part, General, that would require a fair amount of knowledge about the activities at a particular time within the corps so that you could make that assessment as to whether the artillery was being properly deployed and so forth; is that fair to say?" And your response was: "I should just like to add that after taking over these duties, some 15 to 20 days afterwards, I managed to tour all the corps and to size up the situation on the spot to see the state of the artillery and how it was grouped. And on the basis of that, and later on during the operations where I was present, I was able to have an overview of the situation and see whether the artillery was used properly or not." So, General, you are clearly talking about other operations where you were doing your job, touring the corps, making sure that artillery was being properly used; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to make a correction. I said that after I received my duty, some 20 days later, I toured all the corps and I analysed the situation in the artillery units, the grouping thereof, and whether artillery is used in accordance with the rules for its use. As far as I was concerned as the artillery chief, the important thing was whether -- or how the artillery in the corps was grouped, the artillery pieces that were directly subordinate to the corps commander. I had the information about the -- all the artillery pieces, but the grouping in the brigades and battalions was within the purview of the artillery chief in the corps or in the brigade, respectively. So I can say with full responsibility that I could only have influenced and I only had time to have influence in the depth of the territory in the corps as far as the use of the corps artillery was concerned; the corps artillery group, if you are aware of the way in which artillery is groups are set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, General, I intend to stay on the topic of the corps artillery, so that's no problem here. I am not going to ask you about some mortar platoon in Bratunac or something like that, okay? Now, one of the reasons why the corps artillery deployment is so important is because it's corps-wide, it has potentially great influence over the area of responsibility because artillery itself can be much more than simply a tactical weapon; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery is of great importance, but only if groups are set up properly. And in the corps, in light of the size of the area, the corps artillery group, if it comprises one artillery battalion, can only provide support to the main force, to the main body of troops, not to the whole area of responsibility of the corps. And if it were to be deployed in this manner, then the corps artillery could not be under anyone's command. Nobody could exercise command properly over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, General. That's why it was so important for you to be able to make sure that that corps artillery, be it the Drina Corps or the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, artillery groups were properly positioned and being properly used?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Not directly, because I could not have any influence. I could suggest, I could recommend, but the corps commander decided ultimately whether it would be done in this manner or not on the basis of the proposal submitted to him by his artillery chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about that issue for a couple of moments. You told us yesterday, General, how the air bombs, the avio bombe, were made; and you were clear and quick to point out that you understood that they were legal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, I think, in answer to a question from my friend from the Miletic team, you, yourself, said that these bombs were primitively made, they weren't precise, and very often there were very large deviations from one projectile to the other. That was at page 29.062. But, General, these bombs were used by General Dragomir Milosevic's Sarajevo Romanija Corps during the same time you were chief of artillery of the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. No approval was sought from the Main Staff for its use, but he could decide on his own independently whether to use it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, is it your testimony that there was no Main Staff control over the use of air bombs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The use of air bombs is, again, subject to the same rules as the use of other artillery pieces. So the Main Staff could not, in fact not even the corps, could keep records at all times and know at all times whether an air bomb was used in a sector. What it would be like for the chief of the Main Staff or the artillery chief to monitor and to the follow the use of all artillery pieces and air bombs are, in fact, just another artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General. Well, I could show you an order from June of 1994 that specifically deals with the Main Staff's insistence on controlling the use of air bombs, in particular in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I can get that later and show it to you after the break, but let me just move on on this topic. Given the nature of these air bombs being imprecise, hard to guide, General, weren't they used as a tool of terror on the civilian population of Sarajevo by Dragomir Milosevic and his Sarajevo Romanija Corps during the time-period while you were chief of artillery?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became the artillery chief on the 20th of August, 2004. Now, whether air bombs were used in this manner that you just described, well, I can't give you answer because I was not present. I did not have any influence over whether they would be used or not; and I don't know, in fact, who from the Main Staff could exert any influence on whether they would be used in Sarajevo or not. You mentioned the 20th of June; it's much earlier than the 20th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just so you know, the period of time for which General Milosevic faced charges was August of 1994 through November of 1995. So I think that coincides pretty closely with your tenure as chief of artillery of the Main Staff. But, based on your answer, General, concerning your knowledge or lack of knowledge regarding the use of the air bombs, let me just share something with you. It's from the trial judgment in the Galic -- sorry, in the Dragomir Milosevic case. This judgment is dated 12 November 2007. I just want to read to you one of the Trial Chamber's findings. This is at page 323, paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, can I ask the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The relevance, Mr. President, is credibility of this witness, it goes directly to his credibility, it goes to his credibility concerning his answers about what he knew was going on, his control --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We heard his evidence relating to the bombing, shelling, in Sarajevo. Can we move on to another subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have P03785.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 3785. Bear with us, we're trying to get up the right map. Mr. President, if the we may go old school and use the ELMO with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: For my colleagues, this is the excerpt from the Susica artillery plan that we've seen before. For some reason, we can't get it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, have a look at -- at this map. If you want look at the hard copy that's on the ELMO, if that's easier, please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please move it a little bit, because I can only see the target list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you want, you can just pick it up and actually look at it if that will be easier to acquaint yourself with it. You can open the whole thing up, General, it will just a moment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: As you can see, that's an artillery plan or an excerpt from an artillery plan for Operation Susica. This, I can tell you, was planned in 1995. We can see that from a related map which talks about forces that would be freed up once Operation Spreca was completed. So I think that helps put a time-frame on this map. My question to you, General, is: Do you see the firing table?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see the area of Zepa on the map?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see on the firing table various UNPROFOR checkpoints being listed as targets with specific fire signs or call signs to the right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I can see it in the firing table.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as chief of artillery of the Main Staff, can you tell us why those UNPROFOR checkpoints themselves are listed as targets with firing signs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In two sentences. The excerpt from the artillery plan is a document that contains the potential targets; and on the basis of that, precise coordinates are provided, and they are used as known points that will assist in determine the actual target. When fire is actually opened, it will very seldom happen that the fire is opened in accordance with the plan -- as envisaged in the plan. The plan is only used in order to be able to quickly establish the coordinates for the target that shows up. To be quite specific, the trig reference points, the elevations, the intersections, the dominant features, the UN checkpoints, are planned as artillery targets, targets for artillery fire, but they are not targets as such automatically. They are there to provide elements for fire to be opened on any target that appears, and that is the -- that lies in the very essence of planning in the artillery. We cannot rule out that a target might appear in the sector where fire was planned to be opened, but automatically they already have all the elements in place in time. But in most cases, targets appear in the immediate vicinity or at a short distance, enabling the artillery men to fire on those targets on the basis of the elements that are prerecorded, that already exist in the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer. In order for us to follow the map, why don't we try 65 ter 2884.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it is there, but ... Is this the one, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is the original, Mr. President. The version that General Masal is looking at actually has an English translation with it, but this is the original that he was looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We seem to have a translation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We do, Mr. President. We had looked at it before and I thought I had the right 65 ter number, so I apologise that we are not able to get that on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But I just have one last question for you on this topic, General. Isn't it also the case that by 1995 the VRS, in fact, regarded UNPROFOR as a hostile force and that these targets of these checkpoints in Zepa represented the VRS's recognition that they might have to fire directly on UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two fires that were planned to be opened in sectors where there were UNPROFOR checkpoints, in actual combat situation, could have been positions of the enemy forces, not of UNPROFOR; or, for instance, if the enemy forces appeared in the vicinity of this sector, this was planned not because of UNPROFOR, because to make it faster for the fire to be transferred from the point where elements already existed to the target that had just appeared. I am now in the shoes of the artillery chief who drafted this. The UNPROFOR checkpoint was not an enemy target at all. It is merely a sector where the enemy force might -- an enemy target may appear in its immediate or close vicinity. And the claim that in the Main Staff or in the VRS, UNPROFOR was the enemy is simply not valid, or at least to my knowledge it's not valid, because the prevailing opinion in the VRS was that UNPROFOR was not carrying out mission. In many cases, it went against the mandate it had received. It did not operate in accordance with this mandate. That was the position, but I did not share with you this view that you just put to me that they were considered the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General. Let's move off the maps and go back to Visegrad. You assumed your command of the Visegrad tactical group in early February of 1993, I take it, you told us 4 February, and remained there until 20 August of 1994. I think you told us that your area included Rogatica, Visegrad, Rudo, Cajnice, and Gorazde. Do I have that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you assumed that command, you held the rank of full colonel; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You recorded to General Zivanovic as Drina Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was subordinate to General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And which units were subordinated to you, General, when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five brigades: The 1st Podrinje Brigade in Rogatica, the 2nd Podrinje Brigade in Visegrad, the 3rd Podrinje Brigade in Cajnice, the 4th Podrinje Brigade in Rudo, and the 5th Podrinje Brigade -- the Gorazde brigade which was not, in fact, in Gorazde because Gorazde was under the Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you could just clarify, for us, just one issue, as briefly as you can, General: How did the command and control operate when you were in command of this tactical group in terms of the reporting? Were these brigades still reporting directly and subordinate to General Zivanovic, or would they report to you and then you would report on to General Zivanovic? How did that work? Can you just give us an idea, because as you've told us, there were already established brigades with a command structure, and then there is you over them.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commands were subordinate to me. To make this clear, the tactical group was just a temporary force. It is not a permanent unit like brigades or corps or companies or battalions. It is a temporary command that unifies a combat operations in the area of responsibility of some units. The brigade commands were subordinate to me; and in some situations and when it came to some issues, they also reported directly to the corps command. For instance, if a report about UNPROFOR movements had to be sent quickly and directly, then it was sent directly to the Drina Corps, too. But combat reports were sent to me, to the command of the tactical group, and I in turn reported to the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, do you know who Milan Lukic is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of Milan Lukic, and I even met him once.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. It's hard a to talk about Visegrad during this period of time without talking about Milan Lukic; is that fair to say, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you on that. Visegrad was not Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's go into private session for a moment, if we could, Mr. President, and I want to show you a couple of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, earlier on in your testimony, you mentioned an individual named Luka Dragicevic. He served under you; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of the Visegrad brigade; the 2nd Podrinje Brigade, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did he ever tell you about his encounters or experiences with Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in any great detail. On one occasion when I met Milan Lukic on the street, I asked Luka Dragicevic about Milan Lukic, and he just gave me a few sentences to explain who that was. This was not a topic of discussion between allow Luka Dragicevic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Dragicevic tell you about who Milan Lukic was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just briefly, he told me that he had his own group and that he sometimes experienced problems with him when it came to military duties and subordination to the brigade command as the official military formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Lukic eventually become absorbed, as it were, subordinated to the army at some point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever I was informed about the activities of the Visegrad Brigade, I never had the occasion to see either Milan Lukic or his associates in any of the operations or actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, my question was a little bit more simple: Did you ever become aware that Mr. Lukic and his group ultimately subordinated themselves to the VRS? Whether you saw them in any operation or report or not, did you ever become aware that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. Nobody ever told me anything like that. Commander Dragicevic never reported to me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General. I want to move to a new area and try to pick up the pace a little bit. You just mentioned Operation Sword, Operation Mac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see 5D1169, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, you were shown this combat order dated 22 May 1993 during your examination-in-chief. I just wanted to clarify a couple of things about it, partly because I think part of this combat order was not translated into English, and I wanted to ask you a couple of questions to clarify the record. I think my -- my learned friend from the Pandurevic team asked you about Mac 1 or Mac 2, there being a couple of operations Mac. Do you recall there being more than one Mac, or do you recall only one Operation Sword?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two. This was the first one which was ever carried out, and the second was launched but was never completed. Some 15 days into the operation -- actually, the combat operations went on for maybe two or three days from the direction of Cajnice, but the operation was then called off.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you're referring to Mac 1 or Mac 2, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mac 2. Mac 2 was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So it's Sword 1 which went on for a few days, but then was terminated. Do I have that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sword 1 is the one that was ordered, and we are looking at the order. It was completed, it was carried through. Sword 2, Mac 2, was launched 15 days subsequently. It went on for a few days, two or three, but it was called off, it was never completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Glad I've asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can we go to page 2. That's page 2 of the original and page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The English translation says: "Carry out this operation in two stages of eight to ten days," And then it refers to the first stage taking five to six days. But I think that you will agree, General, that when we look at the B/C/S original that you're reading, that English translation is incorrect. So I would just ask you to read for us what the actual order entailed for Mac 1 with respect to these two stages. If you could just read that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, please, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the first stage, which should take three to four days, breakup enemy forces in a rigorous force in the Brodar area of Ustipraca and Medjedja, on the right bank of the Drina and on the left banks of the Drina and Praca rivers, in the Ustipraca Brodar section. During the second stage, which should take between five and six days, regroup forces and use the circular bases, introduce fresh forces, and continue a vigorous attack towards Gorazde. Take the elevations that are around Gorazde as soon as possible and encircle it; thus, creating conditions to disarm the remaining Muslim formations and allow the civilian population to move out to Central Bosnia or to remain in town on a condition that they recognise the Serbian authority."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that the first paragraph is omitted in English translation. That's what you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, and then the second paragraph where it says "In the first stage ..." in the English translation is just wrong because it's obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- misunderstood something there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as we can see from the title of this combat order, it's for the liberation of the general area of Gorazde. And that was the objective of Mac 1, correct, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the objective of the operation; however, the objective was not fully achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to became 8 of the English please, and this will be the last page of the B/C/S, page 5. And it's at the top of both pages that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, do you see there is a reference to the logistics sector of the Main Staff securing the required quantities of fuel and means of explosives?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a request by the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in paragraph 8, the order states: "In the organisation of communications, rely on the exhumations system of the Visegrad tactical group ..." And then it says: "Organise a separate mobile ..." and then there are the initials CV; I believe that stands for a communications centre, "... to be deployed in the Borike section of Rogatica. And I just note that that's been mistranslated. If we look at the original, it is Borike and not Bork. Do you see that section, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, have you been to Borike, General? Can you tell us what's there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Borike. It's a village. There is a motel there in a forest. There is a villa type house; and maybe a kilometre away from there, there is a very famous horse breeding farm known as the Farm at Borike. And that is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, what did this Main Staff communications centre at Borike consist of? Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mobile communications centre is actually the staff vehicle; it's the establishment vehicle. It's a van that houses the communications maze which allows for communication to be established for any location where that vehicle may be. That's why it's called mobile communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who exactly is going to be manning that van or in that van or accompanying that van?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officers and soldiers who belong to the communications branch, who were trained to establish and maintain communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And for the Main Staff communications centre, what unit are they going to be from? Let me put it concretely, in this operation, do you recall where they are from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I've never asked them. I don't know whether they were from the communications regiment of the Main Staff or the Drina Corps, but, obviously, an order had been issued to prepare the communications centre for the IKM of the Main Staff. I never had an opportunity to inquire what unit that actually belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, just one last question on this document before the break. The reason that Gorazde alone is the objective of this combat order, and not Gorazde and Zepa together, is that Zepa had just been declared a UN safe area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Combat activities around Zepa finished 20 days or a month before at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see we are approaching the break. May I suggest we take it now, and I'll move on to a new document when we get back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask how much longer do you have for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I am going to require pretty close to the full four hours that I had estimated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll see. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning again, General. Earlier this morning, when we were talking about the air bombs, I mentioned an order that I was going to put my hands on during the break. I've done so, I've handed out hard copies for my friends, and we have Chamber for the Chamber at hard copy had. I don't think we've managed to load it into e-court yet, but I just wanted to -- and I have a copy for you, too, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: For the record, we've given this 65 ter number 3981.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Take a moment and read this, if you will, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out loud or just to myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Read it to yourself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, this 12 June 1994 document makes it clear, does it not, that the VRS Main Staff decides on the use of air bombs exclusively?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exclusively. Possibly the corps subject to the approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Correct, General, but it has to have Main Staff approval, the corps does, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So the ultimate authority rests in the Main Staff according to this document that we're looking at, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that this predated your duties as chief of artillery for the Main Staff, but is it your testimony that you never became aware, during your entire service in the Main Staff as chief of artillery, that the Main Staff had the ultimate authority and the only authority regarding the use of these air bombs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order, I see now; but as to whether the Main Staff decides or approves the corps commands to use air bombs, there is a document that I drafted to that effect, that the use of air bombs is approved for the use of the Drina and East Bosnian Corps for the Spreca Operation. So obviously that order, too, shows that the Main Staff did decide when to approve the use of air bombs to a particular corps. Now, whether the corps commands or the brigades commands really abided by this, I believe they did. But there may have been some arbitrary actions taken on their own initiative, but I can't tell you that for fact because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General. Let's go back to where we left off before the break, May of 1993. You talked to us about Operation Sword 1. That combat order was dated 22 May. I want to talk about another combat order that was issued on the 1st of May, a nearly identical combat order to that of Sword 1 that ordered the liberation of Gorazde and Zepa. And that was Operation Spring 93. Do you remember that operation, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before the break, I told you that 20 days or a month before this operation, an operation was conducted to liberate Zepa. That operation had ended, and then the order was drafted to liberate Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. And you testified just before we broke that the fighting around Zepa had stopped at a certain time. How long was Operation Spring underway before it stopped, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically, but I think about ten days or so; maybe even less.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, may we have 65 ter 2742 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just quickly, looking at this front page of this combat order for the liberation of Zepa and Gorazde, we can see that it's addressed to various commands including the command of the Visegrad tactical group. Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to page 15 of the English and 9 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to a couple of items on those pages. If we look at paragraph 8 on your version, and it's what's showing on the English version as well, do you see where it says: "In the organisation of communications, take the example of communications of the TG Visegrad ..." And a little bit further down it says: "Communication shall be provided with the Foca TG and the Visegrad TG ..." Do you see those entries, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe what your involvement with this operation was, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of my brigades took part in this operation, the 1st Podrinje Brigade from Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back to page 8 of the English, and this will be the bottom of the page 5 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At the bottom of your page, General, it says: "The Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska shall coordinate the operation from the IKM in Rogatica. Colonel Dragutin Ilic shall be responsible for merging, planning, linking, and command and control of the forces engaged in the liberation of Gorazde, and Colonel Radivoje Miletic of the forces engaged in the liberation of Zepa." Now, General, given that then-Colonel Miletic was going to play a significant command and control role in this operation, and, as you said your forces were involved and your coms, what contacts did you have with then-Colonel Miletic after receiving this order or, indeed, during the course of this operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since my tactical unit as a whole did not take part, it was just the 1st Podrinje Brigade, all the tasks and all the orders that were received from the Drina Corps command were received by the brigade commander. I attended one meeting in the course of the preparations for the operation. The mainstay of this operation was the Drina Corps command. They were the main responsible agent. And the merging or the unification, since some of the headquarters units from the Main Staff, the TG Foca, and the Protection Regiment also used, then the Main Staff from Rogatica command post unified and coordinated the activities around Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell us where then-Colonel Miletic's forward command post was physically located? Where was he working out of during this operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation was under the direct control of the Drina Corps command -- or, rather ... THE INTERPRETER. ... under direct command; interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for control and direction, it went for the Main Staff. I attended a meeting that was chaired by General Milovanovic in the course of the preparations. That was at the command post of the 1st Podrinje Brigade in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, my question to you, General, was: Where was then-Colonel Miletic physically located during this operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only time that I saw Colonel Miletic and the others from the Main Staff, it was at the command post of the 1st Brigade in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was then-Colonel Miletic doing when you saw him there? What was his role?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting that I attended, I don't recall that anyone actually said anything apart from the Drina Corps commander and the chief of the Main Staff. The commander of the Drina Corps briefly outlined the concept of the operation, and General Milovanovic accepted that and also issued some supplementary.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your experience during this operation, it was carried out consistently with what we just saw in the combat order; that is, in terms of then-Colonel Miletic's role, in actual practice in the operation, the role that was ascribed to him in the combat order is actually what he performed during the operation. Do I understand your testimony correctly there, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order stipulates that a team from the Main Staff headed by Colonel Miletic at Zepa shall coordinate, plan, and harmonize activities. This team did not command the operation. The person in charge of the units that were actually carrying out the actions was in command, and that was the Drina Corps commander and his subordinate commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so then just, if you can tell us, what was then-Colonel Miletic's role, just so we are clear?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say on the basis of my experience, of things that I did when I was in a similar role, and that's coordination and organisation of the cooperation and concerted action between units from different corps, and perhaps providing some suggestions in the course of the operation itself to subordinate commanders, all this on the basis of the order from the Main Staff commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General, let's go to a new topic. You testified on Friday, and this was at page 0928 of the transcript, and I quote: "In every territory which was being liberated, the Muslim population was given the option of staying; but if they decided to leave and move to territories under the control of their army, they could do so." Do I have that correct, General, that that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we've seen in a couple of these documents from 1993 that if the Muslims want to stay where they are, they have to recognise Serbian authority. Can you tell us what that entailed? What does that mean "recognizing Serbian authority," General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also said that in practice, I had not encountered a case where I would liberate a territory with my unit and then encounter Muslim population there; but it is quite clear that the decision of the Supreme Command and of the Main Staff made it possible for the population to make a choice, either to move to the territory controlled by their army or to remain abiding by the Serb authority. So nothing more and nothing less than the Serb population had as their rights and obligations. And in this sense, this explains what I said that for over three years in our area of responsibility, we had four Muslims villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the Muslims men, for example, that chose to stay in Serb-held territory. Were they required to serve in the VRS; did they have, instead, a work obligation; or were they just free to live their lives without any war-related obligations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of my command in Visegrad, I did not have any such cases. But while I was the commander of the garrison and of the artillery regiment in Bijeljina, which was part of East Bosnian Corps, I know that a battalion was set up and troops were of Muslims ethnic background. They took part in the fighting as did the Serb units, side by side with them. No distinction was ever made. Those who were unable to serve at the front line were made part of the work obligation, just as Serb males who were not subject to the military obligation. Military obligation or conscription was a general one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So with respect to these four villages that you told us about, what was supposed to happen to the military aged men that were living this in terms of their military service? I understand you've told us about some Muslim fighters that were, I presume, united with their Serb neighbours against whom, I presume, are Croatian forces, up in the eastern Bosnia corps. But how about down in your four villages, General, what about the males of military age in those villages? What was their obligation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a very brief correction, it was not the Muslims who took part in the fighting against Croats side by side with the Serbs; they also served at the front lines facing the Muslim army. And as regards the four villages, I know for a fact that two soldiers, the Golic brothers, who served in the 1st Podrinje Brigade from the very beginning of the war. I think that from those villages -- that the men from those villages did not take part in combat operations, and they were not part of the work obligation units that were engaged at the front line as far as I know. There were some work duty obligations in town; and, there, side by side with elderly Serb men, they worked on those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were those Muslim men -- other than the Golic brothers that you mentioned, were those Muslim men who stayed in those four villages allowed to own weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why not, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the distribution of weapons that would be held or kept in the depth of the territory would have been inappropriate; and, after all, the Serb population in the free territory did not have - I am talking about civilians - did not have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No hunting rifles, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there probably were some hunting rifles. I don't know whether there were any in the Muslims villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at 65 ter 3971, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is an analysis of combat readiness in the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, otherwise known as the Rogatica Brigade. This was conducted by then-Major Kusic, and it's dated February 25th of 1993. I just want to ask you one question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's on page 4 of the English; page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'll just read this to you quickly. He states that, during this period of time, and I quote, "Further activities included disarming of Muslims in the villages of Setorovici, Okruglo, and Osovo, and separating them from Ustasha formations." My question is: Is that consistent with what you saw when you arrived in this area, that the army had disarmed the Muslims in those villages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can conclude, this is not about these villages. We are talking about a period which started with the beginning of the war and ended on the 31st of December, 1992. This is about the disarming of Muslims formations in other villages, in all the villages of Rogatica municipality. These four villages are not expressly mentioned. All the other villages are mentioned, and those may include the four in here. Whether there were weapons or not, I can't tell you with any degree of reliability because I was not in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's just look at the original document, sir. Do you see where it specifically says, and it's just about a little more than halfway down the document: "Further activities included disarming of Muslims in the villages of Setorovici, Okruglo, and Osovo, and separating them from Ustasha formations," and this is for the period of 1992. Isn't that what this just plainly says, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see this. I only saw where it says "in the villages ..." Then further on, it says "Further activities ..." I suppose that I implies that they will be disarmed and separated from Ustasha formations, and the reason for that might be that these villages decided to remain loyal to the Serb authorities and to remain living in the villages; I am talking about the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, so, isn't it the case, then, General, that in order for them, those four villages, to live in the villages, loyal to the Serb authorities, they had to be disarmed? Just a simple question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the answer is simple. No single commander would allow people in his territory, in four villages, to be armed. The civilian police was in charge of the safety of the population; the civilian police of the municipality of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, then, is it your testimony, General, that the Serb population was also disarmed throughout this area that you were responsible for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer for the civilian population is yes; and the answer for the military, the soldiers, is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So if Serb civilians in those areas had hunting rifles, would they be subject to arrest and imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for the hunting rifles that they had a license to carry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to just give the Trial Chamber an idea of how many people we are talking about in these villages. I looked at the 1991 census information, and let me just share with you what I found and see if this corresponds with your knowledge of those villages. According to the census info that I have, Burati had 68 Muslims and 16 Serbs; Okruglo had 95 Muslims and 36 Serbs; Oslovo had 149 Muslims and 169 Serbs; and Setorovici had 112 Muslims and no Serbs; for a total 424 Muslims and 221 Serbs. Do those numbers sound right to you in terms of the numbers we are talking about in these four villages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't as many; there were between 200 and 250. I believe that between 1991 and 1992, a number of them had moved out or were working somewhere else and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that would be not surprising, and, again, you are talking about the Muslims in these villages; correct, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that these Muslims lived peacefully in these villages and that they lived there until the second half of 1994 peacefully, and that they moved away probably in the direction of Sarajevo or somewhere in Central Bosnia. You said that at page 29.030. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a man from Setorovici named Ibro Konakovic? Does that name ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He says in a statement to the Sarajevo SDB --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 3979, if any of my friends want to follow. But I am going to save a little bit of time and just move through this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He says that on 21 November of 1993, Major Kusic went to Setorovici and Osovo, and told the military aged men to report to the school at Okruglo where the command post was based. Then he says that the Muslims' houses were searched, and that they were told by Major Kusic to hand over their guns or they would be shot on the spot. Then, final, he says that about 20 guns and rifles were handed over, their owners were beaten; and then when the men reported to the school, as ordered, 73 men were trucked to the Rasadnik prison near Rogatica, and that some were released, about 10 the next day, but the rest remained in the prison until they were released in July 1994. General, do you know anything about what Mr. Konakovic is talking about, and why these men were put in prison, 73 men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see 65 ter 3977 please. Unfortunately, we don't have an English translation, but it is a short combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'll just ask you, General, to take a look at that if you would, and read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Thayer, just to let you know that we are going to have a break at quarter past 12.00 for 20 minutes, and we will adjourn for the day at half past 1.00. I would like you to try to do your best to conclude before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before 12.15, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the date of this, and this is a regular combat report from yourself to the Drina Corps command - and there seems to be a hole punched - but it look to he many like the date of this is November 21. I think I can see the bottom of a 2 and the bottom of a 1 there. Can we agree on that, that that's the day of this report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I can see number 11 standing for November 1993, but I'm not sure about the actual date.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what this daily combat report says?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report. It says that in cooperation with the SAJ -- SJB Rogatica members, control was carried out in the villages, two people were discovered hiding, and also quite a quantity of automatic weapons was discovered. These two people were disarmed and the weapons were ceased. If I may explain, I can see that there is my signature at the bottom, but I am sure that I don't know anything about this incident. I suppose that the combat report was written, signed by the Chief of Staff, because if this is either the 20 or the 21st of November, I was most probably not in the area of the tactical group because that is around my birthday. I suppose I was absent. There is no other reason for me to deny any knowledge of the event. But the fact that I was probably absent from the area of responsibility, that's why I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General. Well, I can save a little bit of time and I can tell you that I've got a number of other statements from people from Setorovici, from Osovo, all men, one of whom was over 60 at the time he was arrested. That man's name was Muradif Hodzic. Do you know Muradif Hodzic, General, born 11 September 1930?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Save for the retired General Asim Hodzic, I did not know anybody in these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, he said that in about April 1992, he moved from Rogatica to Setorovici because Rajko Kusic began mistreating the Muslims then. I've got other statements from other individuals from these villages who also talk about being arrested on 21 November, and on other occasions, and taken to the Rasadnik prison; and then on to Kula prison in Sarajevo where they were exchanged, in one case over a hundred people. Do you know anything about that, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I've already told you that I was never informed about any of the arrests that took place in these four villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that in the fall of 1994, Muslims were moved out of Setorovici and Serb civilians were moved in? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that they had been moved out, that they wanted to move out, and that they moved out in an organised manner. I don't know when that was. It may have been at the time when I had already left for the General Staff -- rather, the Main Staff. I also know that when they expressed their wish to move out, this met with some resistance. In Sarajevo, they did not want to take them, there were certain problems, some delays and procrastination when it came to their transfer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were shown the other day -- we've spoken about Rajko Kusic a few times, and you were shown a document where he was requesting that the local police provide some protection for these villages because they were being harassed. That was in -- sometime in 1994. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this document, and I learned from Major Kusic that he had intervened and he had requested from the civilian authorities to send more frequent civilian police patrols to protect the population in the four villages in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 3968, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I know -- I know this is a little hard to read. What it is, if you look in the upper right-hand corner, it's a letter to Avdo Palic, March 1993, and this is a letter written by Rajko Kusic. I want to draw your attention to page 2 of this letter and just ask you some questions about it. I want to draw your attention to the sentence that says, "The Americans will not come to defend you ..." If you could just orient yourself to that portion of the letter, where it says, "The Americans will not come to defend you ..." Its towards the top, I think, maybe the one, two, three, fourth line down. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. From there the letter continues, Kusic writes, and I quote: "Look what happened to Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica. Diplomatic help is feeble. They perished. Trnopolje is surrounded, as is Medjedja. Every day they are perishing, but every day they are running towards Jahorina. Where will you go? You still have a little time left to make the right decision. I am not an enemy of the Muslim people, but of the criminals among this people and of those who want to have slaves. The Serbs were the first to have a state, and we have it again. There is no more living together. I suppose this is clear to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can scroll down. A little bit more, please. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "Your people will honour you if you make the right decision, and I suggest to you quit the fighting in a jungle. Take your people to economic centres. You cannot stay on the border to Serbia to separate us from our people. This must be clear to you. You chose the wrong place to fight. The titles of authority in Zepa are small. Go with your people to the place you belong to in Central Bosnia while there is still time. Use the corridors which are opening. Leave the American food; it won't do you any good. Do not accept charity, but try to give it away. Europe does not allow Islam to go on, don't you see that? Big politics is going deep. Leave the weapons, organise the people for salvation, and leave Zepa or become loyal. This is your last chance." General, Major Kusic was your subordinate during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Does this letter reflect your understanding of the VRS policy towards the Muslim population in your area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking for me to dwell upon the letter that Major Kusic wrote to Avdo Palic, it's pointless. Major Kusic was my subordinate. He performed military tasks that I ordered him to perform. What he wrote to somebody or what he kept in his head, what he thought of, I really wouldn't be able to tell you. I don't know. In any case, this was not part of the policies of the army of Republika Srpska in the -- in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, what part do you disagree with, sir? If what was just read to you does not reflect your understanding of the VRS policy towards the Muslim population in your area, what part of that do you disagree with or did you disagree with at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with the letter. I really don't know why a commander would exchange letters with the opposing side's commander. I had an opportunity to legally talk to their commander, but we never exchanged any letters, and that's why I don't agree with the letter. I don't agree with the form, because a letter is not a military form. If he had consulted me, asking whether to send this letter or not, or if he had shown it to me, I am sure I would not have agreed to that. This is just a piece of paper and a heap of sentences on that paper that have absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with the combat or any military tasks for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I am not talking about form or the propriety of commanders exchanging letters. What I am asking you is, based on what is written here by this VRS commander, to the commander of the Muslim forces, what is it in that section, can you point out to the Trial Chamber, that I read on you to the that you disagree with? I am not talking about just the fact that a letter was written, and you can't identify anything that you don't agree with, then just say so and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without necessarily having to hear from Madam Fauveau, have we not heard enough? Can we not move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If the Court wishes, I will move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Based on your testimony, General, were you in the western front from late May 1995 continually through October of that year, or were you going back and forth to various locations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was mostly in Krajina in the western front. I may have gone home for a couple of days, but I wouldn't be sure of that, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But during that period of time, you weren't beside any IKMs or any other specific assignments. You were, for all intents and purposes, in the Krajina full time from late May through October of 1995; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be crystal clear, when did you leave the Krajina? Was it in October, was it in November, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was in October, but again I don't know the date. I can't even give you any specific longer period of time. I believe that it was in October. It was about that time that we all withdrew to the Main Staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I can help you out a little bit with some dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Ma we see 5D999 please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: As you can see, we've got Directive 9 up. It's dated 28 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You talked about this directive relatively recently, General, and I presume that you reviewed it in the course of your proofing; do I have that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. In this directive, General, there is no mention of MUP forces being part of Operation Stit 95, Operation Shield; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: MUP forces are not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did MUP forces participate in this operation, specifically during the counter-attack that you spoke about the other day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's be clear on one thing. This operation never took place; it was never carried out. The intention of the Main Staff was one thing, i.e., the decision of the commander and his idea was one thing. The situation on the territory throughout the next few days was something completely different. Very soon, we encountered major problems on the front line, so we were mainly engaged in defence. During my first stage -- stay in Krajina from October -- the end of October 2004 to mid-March, yes, there were also MUP forces there, the police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just for clarification of the record, the transcript shows October 2004 to mid-March, can you please just clarify General what dates you are talking about. I presume it's not 2004.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about 2004. My first departure for the IKM in Jasenica with General Milovanovic and General Jovo Maric was the end of October 2004 and my stay there until the second half of March 1995. During the combat at the time, we also had some MUP forces attached to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I will just go right to it. We are talking about 1994 and 1995 are we not, not 2004 and 2005?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I misspoke, obviously. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
